title: Colloquium: Simulating non-Markovian Dynamics In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, And J. Ankerhold
abstract:
Author(s): Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, and J. Ankerhold

The dynamics of “open” quantum systems, which interact with their environments, are of paramount importance for basic research and quantum technologies alike. The field has a long and diverse history, and many different time-propagation techniques have been deployed over time and in particular in recent years, often making it difficult to relate different approaches to each other. Based on a unified framework, this Colloquium provides an overview of methods used to describe and to simulate open quantum systems in various contexts, including quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, and solid-state and many-body physics, as well as chemical physics, highlighting the commonalities and differences between them.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021002] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium provides a unified framework for simulating non-Markovian open quantum systems, covering various methods and their applications across quantum physics.
motivation: Open quantum systems are crucial for quantum technologies, but non-Markovian dynamics are challenging to simulate. The authors aim to organize and relate the many existing techniques.
method: The paper reviews and categorizes simulation methods for non-Markovian open quantum systems within a unified framework, highlighting commonalities and differences.
result: It offers a comprehensive overview of methods, including their applicability in quantum optics, quantum information, thermodynamics, and solid-state physics.
conclusion: The unified framework helps researchers choose appropriate simulation techniques and fosters cross-disciplinary understanding.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review of space-time duality in quantum many-body dynamics, focusing on brickwork quantum circuits and their connection to quantum computation.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult; space-time duality offers a unified approach by treating space and time on equal footing.
method: The review synthesizes recent advances in discretized time evolution, emphasizing brickwork quantum circuits and the analogy with digital computation.
result: Provides a unified view of dynamical evolution in quantum many-body systems, highlighting exactly solvable models and the role of space-time duality.
conclusion: Space-time duality is a powerful tool for understanding quantum dynamics, with deep connections to quantum computation and potential for future developments.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: This review covers nonequilibrium dynamics in photoexcited Mott insulators, focusing on metastable states and control via strong fields.
motivation: Understanding nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated systems can reveal new ways to control material properties and uncover novel quantum phases.
method: The paper is a comprehensive review summarizing recent theoretical and experimental advances, discussing mechanisms and pathways for driving Mott insulators out of equilibrium.
result: It highlights key mechanisms for photodoped carrier evolution and the emergence of metastable states with superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.
conclusion: Photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators offer a rich platform for exploring quantum thermodynamics and information processing, though the review is more focused on condensed matter physics.

title: Quantum Resource Comparison For Two Leading Surface Code Lattice Surgery Approaches
authors: Tyler Leblond And Ryan S. Bennink
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2187 (2026).

Hamiltonian simulation is one of the most promising candidates for the demonstration of quantum advantage within the next ten years, and several studies have proposed end-to-end resource estimates for executing such algorithms on fault-tolerant quantum processors. Usually, these resource estimates are based upon the assumption that quantum error correction is implemented using the surface code, and that the best surface code compilation scheme involves serializing input circuits by eliminating all Clifford gates. This transformation is thought to make best use of the native multi-body measurement (lattice surgery) instruction set available to surface codes. Some work, however, has suggested that direct compilation from Clifford+T to lattice surgery operations may be beneficial for circuits that have high degrees of logical parallelism. In this study, we analyze the resource costs for implementing Hamiltonian simulation using example approaches from each of these leading surface code compilation families. The Hamiltonians whose dynamics we consider are those of the transverse-field Ising model in several geometries, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the [MATH] complex under a time-varying magnetic field. We show, among other things, that the optimal scheme depends on whether Hamiltonian simulation is implemented using the quantum signal processing or Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, with Trotterization benefiting by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation for these applications. Our results suggest that surface code quantum computers should not have a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme, but that smart compilers should predict the optimal scheme based upon high-level quantities from logical circuits such as average circuit density, numbers of logical qubits, and T fraction.

.
tldr: This paper compares two surface code compilation strategies for Hamiltonian simulation, showing that the optimal approach depends on the simulation algorithm and circuit characteristics.
motivation: To determine whether serializing Clifford gates or direct Clifford+T compilation is more resource-efficient for fault-tolerant quantum computing, as prior work suggested the latter may benefit circuits with high parallelism.
method: The authors analyze resource costs for Hamiltonian simulation of several models (transverse-field Ising, Kitaev honeycomb, and a complex under time-varying field) using quantum signal processing and Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, comparing two compilation families.
result: Trotterization benefits by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation, while the optimal scheme depends on the algorithm and circuit properties like density, qubit count, and T fraction.
conclusion: Surface code quantum computers should use adaptive compilation strategies rather than a one-size-fits-all approach, with smart compilers predicting the best scheme based on high-level circuit metrics.

title: Disorder-Induced Entanglement Phase Transitions In Non-Hermitian Systems With Skin Effects
authors: Kai Li, Ze-Chuan Liu, And Yong Xu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2186 (2026).

Non-Hermitian dynamics is ubiquitous in various physical systems. While recent study shows that such a dynamics leads to an area-law scaling of the entanglement entropy due to the non-Hermitian skin effects, it remains unclear how disorder changes the behavior of the entanglement entropy in a non-Hermitian system with skin effects. Here we study the dynamics of a many-body state of free fermions in the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model with open boundaries, and find that the area-law behavior of the entanglement entropy in the pristine Hatano-Nelson model develops into a logarithmic scaling for small disorder strength. As we further increase the disorder strength, the system reenters an area-law regime through an entanglement phase transition. At the critical point, the entanglement entropy exhibits a universal algebraic scaling. We further demonstrate the absence of a conformal invariance in the log-law regime by examining the subsystem entanglement entropy, the connected correlation function and the mutual information. Finally, we show the existence of disorder induced entanglement phase transitions in the Hatano-Nelson model with periodic boundaries.

.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement phase transitions in a non-Hermitian Hatano-Nelson model with disorder, showing transitions between area-law and logarithmic scaling of entanglement entropy.
motivation: Understanding how disorder affects entanglement dynamics in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects is an open question, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and information processing.
method: The authors numerically study the dynamics of free fermions in the Hatano-Nelson model with open and periodic boundaries, computing entanglement entropy, connected correlation functions, and mutual information for various disorder strengths.
result: They find that disorder induces a transition from area-law to logarithmic scaling of entanglement entropy at small disorder, and back to area-law at larger disorder, with algebraic scaling at criticality. They also show absence of conformal invariance in the log-law regime.
conclusion: Disorder can induce entanglement phase transitions in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects, which may have implications for quantum information processing and thermodynamics in such systems.

title: Promise Of Graph Sparsification And Decomposition For Noise Reduction In Qaoa: Analysis For Trapped-Ion Compilations
authors: Jai Moondra, Phillip C. Lotshaw, Greg Mohler, And Swati Gupta
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2185 (2026).

We develop new approximate compilation schemes that significantly reduce the expense of compiling the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving the Max-Cut problem. Our main focus is on compilation with trapped-ion simulators using Pauli-[MATH] operations and all-to-all Ising Hamiltonian [MATH] evolution generated by Molmer-Sorensen or optical dipole force interactions, though some of our results also apply to standard gate-based compilations. Our results are based on principles of graph sparsification and decomposition; the former reduces the number of edges in a graph while maintaining its cut structure, while the latter breaks a weighted graph into a small number of unweighted graphs. Though these techniques have been used as heuristics in various hybrid quantum algorithms, there have been no guarantees on their performance, to the best of our knowledge. This work provides the first provable guarantees using sparsification and decomposition to improve quantum noise resilience and reduce quantum circuit complexity. For quantum hardware that uses edge-by-edge QAOA compilations, sparsification leads to a direct reduction in circuit complexity. For trapped-ion quantum simulators implementing all-to-all [MATH] pulses, we show that for a [MATH] factor loss in the Max-Cut approximation ([MATH], our compilations improve the (worst-case) number of [MATH] pulses from [MATH] to [MATH] and the (worst-case) number of Pauli-[MATH] bit flips from [MATH] to [MATH] for [MATH]-node graphs. This is an asymptotic improvement for any constant [MATH]. We demonstrate that significant improvements to the approximation ratio are obtained using decomposition in simulated trapped-ion experiments with dephasing noise. We further present a generic argument showing that sparsification results in an exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bound in digital computing schemes based on one- and two-qubit gates, which are relevant to a wide variety of hardwares such as superconducting qubits and certain neutral atom or trapped ion setups, and more sophisticated noise models. We anticipate these approximate compilation techniques will be useful tools in a variety of future quantum computing experiments.

.
tldr: This paper provides provable guarantees for graph sparsification and decomposition to reduce circuit complexity and improve noise resilience in QAOA for Max-Cut, with applications to trapped-ion and gate-based quantum computing.
motivation: QAOA compilation for Max-Cut is resource-intensive and noise-sensitive; existing sparsification/decomposition heuristics lack performance guarantees. The authors aim to provide theoretical foundations and practical improvements.
method: They develop approximate compilation schemes using graph sparsification (reducing edges while preserving cut structure) and decomposition (breaking weighted graphs into unweighted ones), and analyze their impact on circuit complexity and noise resilience for trapped-ion and gate-based implementations.
result: For trapped-ion simulators, they achieve asymptotic improvements in the number of Molmer-Sorensen pulses and Pauli-X bit flips, and demonstrate improved approximation ratios under dephasing noise. They also show exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bounds for digital schemes.
conclusion: The proposed compilation techniques offer provable reductions in circuit complexity and enhanced noise resilience, making them valuable tools for near-term quantum computing experiments.

title: Entanglement Growth In The Dark Intervals Of A Locally Monitored Free-fermion Chain
authors: Giovanni Di Fresco, Youenn Le Gal, Davide Valenti, Marco Schiró, And Angelo Carollo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2183 (2026).

We consider a free fermionic chain with monitoring of the particle density on a single site of the chain and study the entanglement dynamics of quantum jump trajectories. We show that the entanglement entropy grows in time towards a stationary state which display volume law scaling of the entropy, in stark contrast with both the unitary dynamics after a local quench and the no-click limit corresponding to full post-selection. We explain the extensive entanglement growth as a consequence of the peculiar distribution of quantum jumps in time, which display superpoissonian waiting time distribution characterised by a bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals where no-clicks are detected, akin to the distribution of fluorescence light in a driven atom. We show that the presence of dark intervals is the key feature to explain the effect and that by increasing the number of sites which are monitored the volume law scaling gives away to the Zeno effect and its associated area law.

.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement growth in a free-fermion chain under local monitoring, showing that dark intervals between quantum jumps lead to volume-law entanglement, contrasting with unitary and no-click limits.
motivation: Understanding how measurement-induced dynamics affect entanglement in many-body systems is crucial for quantum information and thermodynamics, especially the role of quantum jumps and dark intervals.
method: The authors analyze a free-fermionic chain with single-site density monitoring, using quantum jump trajectories and waiting time distributions to characterize entanglement entropy dynamics.
result: They find that entanglement entropy grows to a stationary state with volume-law scaling, attributed to super-Poissonian waiting times with bunching and long dark intervals; increasing monitored sites leads to Zeno effect and area law.
conclusion: The work highlights the importance of dark intervals in measurement-induced entanglement growth, offering insights into non-equilibrium quantum dynamics and potential implications for quantum thermodynamics.

title: On The Quantum Computational Complexity Of Classical Linear Dynamics With Geometrically Local Interactions: Dequantization And Universality
authors: Kazuki Sakamoto And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2182 (2026).

The simulation of large-scale classical systems in exponentially small space on quantum computers has gained attention. The prior work demonstrated that a quantum algorithm offers an exponential speedup over any classical algorithm in simulating classical dynamics with long-range interactions. However, many real-world classical systems, such as those arising from partial differential equations, exhibit only local interactions. The question remains whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition. In this work, we thoroughly characterize the computational complexity of simulating such geometrically local systems on quantum computers. First, we dequantize the quantum algorithm for simulating short-time (polynomial-time) dynamics of such systems. This implies that the problem of simulating this dynamics does not yield any exponential quantum advantage. Second, we show that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Third, we show that the computational complexity of simulating long-time (exponential-time) dynamics is captured by exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation. This suggests a super-polynomial time advantage when restricting the computation to polynomial-space, or an exponential space advantage otherwise. This work offers new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations, providing a pathway for achieving quantum advantage in practical problems.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the quantum computational complexity of simulating classical linear dynamics with geometrically local interactions, showing no exponential speedup for short-time dynamics but potential advantages for long-time dynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to determine whether quantum computers can provide exponential speedup for simulating classical systems with local interactions, which are common in real-world applications like partial differential equations.
method: They dequantize the quantum algorithm for short-time dynamics, prove hardness results for short-time simulation, and analyze the complexity of long-time dynamics in terms of quantum complexity classes.
result: Short-time dynamics simulation is dequantized (no exponential quantum advantage) and is as hard as polynomial-time linear-space probabilistic classical computation; long-time dynamics is captured by exponential-time polynomial-space quantum computation, suggesting super-polynomial time or exponential space advantages.
conclusion: The work provides a thorough complexity characterization, indicating that quantum advantage for local classical dynamics is limited to long-time simulations or space-restricted settings, offering insights for practical quantum advantage.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: This paper constructs entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved error correction and resource efficiency.
motivation: To develop scalable quantum error-correcting codes with high performance and low entanglement overhead for practical quantum communication and computing.
method: The authors construct EA-QC-QLDPC codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices, analyze code rates, and propose an efficient encoding scheme. They evaluate performance using quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum decoding under depolarizing and Markovian noise.
result: The proposed codes achieve nearly an order of magnitude improvement in error-correction performance compared to layered binary sum-product decoding, and outperform prior works under QBLNMS decoding, handling both random and burst errors.
conclusion: The constructions are scalable and resource-efficient, offering practical advantages for quantum error correction.

title: Atommovr: An Open-source Simulation Framework For Rearrangement In Atomic Arrays
authors: Nikhil K Harle, Bo-Yu Chen, Bob Bao, And Hannes Bernien
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2177 (2026).

The task of atom rearrangement has emerged in the last decade as a fundamental building block in the development of neutral atom-based quantum processors. As such processors grow to thousands of atoms, it becomes increasingly important to design algorithms robust to experimental sources of error. While recent progress has been made towards developing algorithms with favorable time scaling, such work has been limited to noiseless settings. Moreover, there is a lack of open-source code for reproducing and benchmarking existing algorithms. To address these deficiencies, we develop an open-source simulation framework, atommovr, and leverage it to study three distinct settings: 1) time-optimal, noiseless rearrangement, 2) noisy rearrangement under realistic error models, and 3) noiseless dual-species rearrangement. We extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, study advantageous strategies across different error regimes, and develop a novel dual-species algorithm, InsideOut, capable of avoiding 'blocked' configurations with a near-unity success rate. We hope that atommovr can serve as a common tool for the community to study rearrangement, lower the barrier to entry for new experimental groups, and stimulate progress in developing algorithms tailored to minimize atom loss in experiment.

.
tldr: This paper introduces an open-source simulation framework for atom rearrangement in neutral atom arrays, addressing time-optimal, noisy, and dual-species scenarios.
motivation: Atom rearrangement is crucial for neutral atom quantum processors, but existing algorithms lack robustness to experimental errors and there is no open-source benchmarking tool.
method: The authors develop atommovr, a simulation framework, and use it to study time-optimal noiseless rearrangement, noisy rearrangement with realistic error models, and dual-species rearrangement, including a novel algorithm called InsideOut.
result: They extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, identify advantageous strategies across error regimes, and demonstrate that InsideOut avoids blocked configurations with near-unity success rate.
conclusion: atommovr provides a common tool for the community to study and benchmark rearrangement algorithms, potentially accelerating progress in neutral atom quantum computing.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper presents an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits up to hundreds of qubits by combining tensor network contraction with a Markov process, demonstrated on QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits under noise.
motivation: Classical simulation of large quantum circuits is limited by exponential overhead, and approximate methods are often insufficient. The authors aim to provide an exact sampling method that scales to hundreds of qubits, enabling validation of quantum algorithms and noise models at a larger scale.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. This allows exact sampling from the output distribution of ideal and noisy circuits.
result: The method successfully generates samples from QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models, achieving a scale previously out of reach for exact simulation.
conclusion: This work significantly expands the scope of classical simulation for quantum algorithm research, providing a tool to test assumptions and conjectures at larger scales, which is valuable for benchmarking quantum devices and understanding noise effects.

title: Optimal Schedule Of Multi-channel Quantum Zeno Dragging With Application To Solving The k-SAT Problem
authors: Yipei Zhang, Alain Sarlette, Philippe Lewalle, Tathagata Karmakar, Thilo Scharnhorst, And K. Birgitta Whaley
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2167 (2026).

Quantum Zeno dragging enables the preparation of common eigenstates of a set of observables by frequent measurement and adiabatic-like modulation of the measurement basis. In this work, we present a deeper analysis of multi-channel Zeno dragging using generalized measurements, i.e. simultaneously measuring a set of non-commuting observables that vary slowly in time, to drag the state towards a target subspace. For concreteness, we will focus on a measurement-driven approach to solving k-SAT problems as examples. We first compute some analytical upper bounds on the convergence time, including the effect of finite measurement time resolution. We then apply optimal control theory to obtain the optimal dragging schedule that lower bounds the convergence time, for low-dimensional settings. This study provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and its optimization, and also serves as a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks including measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes multi-channel quantum Zeno dragging with generalized measurements and applies optimal control to find schedules that minimize convergence time, with applications to solving k-SAT problems.
motivation: Quantum Zeno dragging can prepare target states via frequent measurements, but multi-channel (non-commuting) measurements and optimal schedules are not well understood. The authors aim to provide a theoretical foundation and optimize dragging for quantum information tasks.
method: They derive analytical upper bounds on convergence time, including finite measurement resolution effects, and use optimal control theory to find optimal dragging schedules in low-dimensional settings.
result: They obtain analytical bounds and optimal schedules that lower bound the convergence time, demonstrating the approach on k-SAT examples.
conclusion: The work provides a foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and its optimization, guiding design of measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

title: Sparse Identification Of Quantum Hamiltonian Dynamics Via Quantum Circuit Learning
authors: Yusei Tateyama And Yuzuru Kato
abstract: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) is a data-driven framework for estimating classical nonlinear dynamical systems from time-series data. In this approach, system dynamics is represented as a linear combination of a predefined set of basis functions, and the corresponding coefficients are sparsely estimated from observed time-series data. In this study, we propose sparse identification of quantum Hamiltonian dynamics (SIQHDy), a SINDy-inspired quantum circuit learning framework for estimating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from time-series data of quantum measurement outcomes. In SIQHDy, the unitary evolution of a quantum Hamiltonian system is expressed as a product of basis quantum circuits, and the corresponding circuit parameters are estimated through sparsity-promoting optimization. We numerically demonstrate that SIQHDy accurately reconstructs the dynamics of single-, three-, and five-spin systems, and exhibits robustness to measurement noise in the three-spin case. Furthermore, we propose an extension of SIQHDy for scenarios with limited accessible observables and evaluate its performance in identifying three-spin systems and in network-structure identification for five-spin systems.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum circuit learning framework inspired by SINDy to sparsely identify quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from measurement time-series data.
motivation: Estimating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from data is crucial for characterizing quantum systems, but existing methods may require many measurements or lack interpretability. The authors aim to adapt classical sparse identification techniques to quantum systems.
method: The method, SIQHDy, represents the unitary evolution as a product of basis quantum circuits and uses sparsity-promoting optimization to estimate circuit parameters from time-series data of measurement outcomes. An extension handles limited observable access.
result: Numerical demonstrations show accurate reconstruction for single-, three-, and five-spin systems, robustness to noise in three-spin case, and successful network-structure identification for five-spin systems.
conclusion: SIQHDy provides a promising data-driven approach for identifying quantum Hamiltonian dynamics, with potential applications in quantum system characterization and network inference.

title: Rotation-enhanced Photonic Spin Hall Effect In A Ring Bose–Einstein Condensate
authors: Leibo Deng, Muqaddar Abbas, Ghaisud Din, Hocine Bahlouli And Yong-Hong Ma
abstract: We show that rotation can strongly amplify the photonic spin Hall effect in a ring Bose–Einstein condensate. For an incident probe beam carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM), the spin-dependent transverse shift of the reflected light is weak in the non-rotating regime but becomes strongly enhanced under rotation because rotation lifts the degeneracy of the condensate mechanical modes via Bragg scattering. The resulting mode splitting produces large photonic spin Hall shifts at ultra-low optical power, with the enhancement increasing with both the condensate winding number and the probe OAM , while remaining weakly affected by atom–atom interactions. Our findings elucidate a rotation-governed mechanism underlying spin-dependent light transport in hybrid atom–optomechanical systems, thereby highlighting its potential for applications in high-precision rotational sensing.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that rotation can strongly enhance the photonic spin Hall effect in a ring Bose-Einstein condensate, enabling large spin-dependent shifts at ultra-low optical power.
motivation: The photonic spin Hall effect is typically weak, and the authors seek a mechanism to amplify it for applications in precision sensing. They explore a hybrid atom-optomechanical system where rotation lifts degeneracy and enhances the effect.
method: The authors theoretically analyze a ring Bose-Einstein condensate coupled to an optical cavity, considering Bragg scattering and mechanical mode splitting induced by rotation. They derive expressions for the spin-dependent transverse shift of reflected light and study its dependence on rotation, winding number, probe OAM, and atom-atom interactions.
result: Rotation strongly enhances the photonic spin Hall shift, with the enhancement increasing with condensate winding number and probe OAM, while being weakly affected by atom-atom interactions. The effect occurs at ultra-low optical power.
conclusion: The findings reveal a rotation-governed mechanism for spin-dependent light transport in hybrid atom-optomechanical systems, with potential for high-precision rotational sensing.

title: Fate Of Entanglement In Open Quantum Spin Liquid: Time Evolution Of Its Genuine Multipartite Negativity Upon Sudden Coupling To A Dissipative Bosonic Environment
authors: Federico Garcia-Gaitan And Branislav K Nikolić
abstract: Many-body entanglement properties of quantum spin liquids (QSLs), persisting at arbitrarily long distances, have been intensely explored over the past two decades, but mostly for QSLs viewed as closed quantum systems. However, in experiments and potential quantum computing applications, candidate materials for this exotic phase of quantum matter will always interact with a dissipative environment, such as the one generated by bosonic quasiparticles in solids at finite temperature. Here we investigate both the stability and spatial distribution of entanglement for the Kitaev model of QSL, which is made open by its sudden coupling to an infinite bosonic bath of Caldeira–Leggett type and then time-evolved in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. From the time-dependent density matrix of QSL subregions, we extract genuine multipartite negativity (GMN), quantum Fisher information, spin–spin correlators, and the expectation value (EV) of the Wilson loop operator. In particular, time dependence of GMN offers the most penetrating insights: (i) in the Markovian regime, it remains nonzero only in hexagonal loopy subregions of QSL (as also discovered very recently for closed QSLs), eventually vanishing on the same timescale on which the EV of the Wilson loop operator vanishes; (ii) in the non-Markovian regime with pronounced memory effects, surprisingly, GMN remains nonzero up to much higher temperatures. In addition, the non-Markovian dynamics generates emergent interactions between spins, thereby opening avenues for tailoring properties of QSL via engineering of dissipation.
tldr: This paper studies the time evolution of genuine multipartite negativity in an open Kitaev quantum spin liquid coupled to a dissipative bosonic environment, revealing that non-Markovian dynamics can preserve entanglement at higher temperatures.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are typically studied as closed systems, but in realistic settings they interact with dissipative environments. Understanding how entanglement behaves under such open dynamics is crucial for quantum computing applications.
method: The authors model the Kitaev spin liquid suddenly coupled to a Caldeira-Leggett bosonic bath and time-evolve the system in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. They compute genuine multipartite negativity, quantum Fisher information, spin-spin correlators, and Wilson loop expectation values from the time-dependent density matrix.
result: In the Markovian regime, genuine multipartite negativity persists only in hexagonal loopy subregions and vanishes on the same timescale as the Wilson loop expectation value. In the non-Markovian regime, negativity remains nonzero up to much higher temperatures, and emergent interactions between spins are generated.
conclusion: The findings suggest that non-Markovian dissipation can stabilize multipartite entanglement in quantum spin liquids, and engineering dissipation could be a route to tailoring their properties.

title: Local Complex Dependence And Separability In Madelung Hydrodynamics
authors: Lorenzo Pirovano
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a many-particle pure state in a fixed position representation, we consider the mixed cross-particle derivatives of the logarithm of the wave function. Their real part is one half of the Holland-Wang local dependence function of the configuration density, while their imaginary part is the cross-Jacobian of the Madelung velocity field. On a node-free product region, vanishing of all cross blocks throughout the region is equivalent to local multiplicative separability. Under Schrodinger evolution with a real scalar potential, the initial growth of a cross block from a separable state is sourced by the corresponding mixed Hessian of the potential and is purely imaginary to first order in time. The construction is a local separability and dependence diagnostic, rather than a basis-independent entanglement measure.
tldr: This paper introduces a local separability diagnostic based on cross-particle derivatives of the log-wavefunction in Madelung hydrodynamics, showing that vanishing cross blocks indicate local multiplicative separability and that initial growth from separable states is sourced by the potential's mixed Hessian.
motivation: To develop a local separability and dependence diagnostic for many-particle quantum states that is not a basis-independent entanglement measure, potentially useful for identifying entanglement structure in specific regions.
method: The authors analyze mixed cross-particle derivatives of the logarithm of the wave function, separating real and imaginary parts, and study their behavior under Schrödinger evolution with a real scalar potential.
result: They prove that vanishing of all cross blocks on a node-free product region is equivalent to local multiplicative separability, and that the initial growth of a cross block from a separable state is purely imaginary and sourced by the mixed Hessian of the potential.
conclusion: The construction provides a local separability and dependence diagnostic, but it is not a basis-independent entanglement measure, limiting its direct applicability to the researcher's core interests.

title: Zero Transfer On Mixed Graphs
authors: Huiqiu Lin Xingkun Song
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate zero transfer on mixed graphs. Zero transfer is a quantum walk phenomenon in which the transition amplitude between two vertices is identically zero for all times, so that no quantum state transfer occurs between them. Using the Hermitian adjacency matrix, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for zero transfer in mixed graphs. We then specialize these criteria to oriented circulant graphs, obtaining nonexistence results for prime order, structural restrictions for even order, and exhaustive computational classifications for small orders.
tldr: This paper studies zero transfer in mixed graphs, a quantum walk phenomenon, using Hermitian adjacency matrices, and provides conditions and classifications for oriented circulant graphs.
motivation: Zero transfer is a fundamental quantum walk property with implications for quantum state transfer and quantum information processing on graphs.
method: The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for zero transfer in mixed graphs using the Hermitian adjacency matrix, then specialize to oriented circulant graphs.
result: They obtain nonexistence results for prime order, structural restrictions for even order, and exhaustive computational classifications for small orders.
conclusion: The work advances the theoretical understanding of quantum walks on mixed graphs, but its direct applicability to the user's core interests is limited.

The authors employ the Hermitian adjacency matrix to model mixed graphs and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for zero transfer. They then specialize these conditions to oriented circulant graphs, a class of vertex-transitive graphs with rotational symmetry. For these graphs, they prove nonexistence results for prime order, establish structural restrictions for even order, and provide exhaustive computational classifications for small orders. The work bridges algebraic graph theory and quantum information science, offering new tools for understanding quantum walk dynamics on non-simple graph structures.

title: Quantum Computing For Industrial Electromagnetics: Applicability And Case Studies In Solving Maxwell's Equations
authors: Francesco Turro, Marco Maronese, Daniele Dragoni
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational electromagnetics plays a central role in many industrial applications but often requires substantial computational resources, particularly when fine spatial discretizations are needed. While classical approaches remain the standard, quantum computing offers the potential to accelerate large-scale simulations by encoding them with a limited number of qubits. Here, we investigate the performance and resource scaling of the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) and Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) algorithms for solving linear systems generated by the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method, a widely adopted numerical scheme for discretizing Maxwell's equations. We benchmark their performance across representative industrial use cases, including radar propagation, lens simulations, and beamforming processes. Our results demonstrate the validity of the approaches, achieving state infidelities smaller than [MATH] with success probabilities greater than [MATH], compatible with practical quantum state sampling. Overall, we observe that the QSVT method consistently delivers higher accuracy. We further observe that the condition number of the linear matrix, a key factor governing the performance of quantum solvers, saturates as the number of spatial lattice points increases. This implies that the spatial grid can be scaled to realistic industrial dimensions without increasing the HHL or QSVT circuit depth due to ill-conditioned matrices.
tldr: This paper benchmarks quantum linear solvers (HHL and QSVT) for solving Maxwell's equations via FDTD, showing feasibility for industrial electromagnetics.
motivation: Industrial electromagnetics simulations are computationally expensive; quantum computing may offer speedups for large-scale problems.
method: The authors apply HHL and QSVT algorithms to linear systems from FDTD discretizations of Maxwell's equations, benchmarking on radar, lens, and beamforming cases.
result: Both algorithms achieve high state infidelities and success probabilities, with QSVT more accurate; condition numbers saturate with grid size, enabling scaling.
conclusion: Quantum solvers are promising for industrial electromagnetics, but current work is a benchmark rather than a novel information-theoretic contribution.

The authors benchmark these quantum solvers on representative industrial use cases, including radar propagation, lens simulations, and beamforming, and report state infidelities below 2e-3 with success probabilities above 1e-3, indicating practical feasibility. A key finding is that the condition number of the FDTD linear matrix saturates as the spatial grid is refined, implying that circuit depth does not grow with problem size due to ill-conditioning, which is crucial for scalability to realistic industrial dimensions. The study provides a comparative analysis showing QSVT consistently outperforms HHL in accuracy.

deep_read.results_analysis: The paper reports state infidelities smaller than 2e-3 and success probabilities greater than 1e-3 for both algorithms across all test cases, with QSVT achieving consistently higher accuracy. These metrics are compatible with practical quantum state sampling, suggesting that the algorithms could be used in near-term quantum devices. The most significant result is the observation that the condition number of the FDTD linear matrix saturates as the number of spatial lattice points increases. This implies that the circuit depth of HHL and QSVT, which scales with the condition number, does not grow with grid refinement, thus allowing the spatial grid to be scaled to realistic industrial dimensions without increasing the computational cost due to ill-conditioning. This is a crucial finding for the feasibility of quantum solvers in computational electromagnetics.
strengths: The paper addresses a practical and important problem (computational electromagnetics) with clear industrial relevance.
The finding on condition number saturation is novel and has significant implications for scalability.
The benchmarking across multiple use cases provides a comprehensive evaluation of the algorithms.
The quantitative performance metrics (infidelity, success probability) are concrete and useful for practitioners.
limitations: The analysis is based on classical simulations of quantum algorithms, not actual quantum hardware, so practical issues like noise and decoherence are not fully addressed.
The paper does not provide a detailed resource estimation (e.g., number of qubits, T-gates) for the industrial-scale problems, which is crucial for assessing practical feasibility.
The condition number saturation is observed empirically; a theoretical proof or deeper analysis of why this occurs is not provided.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics, particularly the application of quantum algorithms to solve classical physics problems. It demonstrates how quantum computing can potentially accelerate computational electromagnetics, a field that relies on solving Maxwell's equations. The use of HHL and QSVT highlights the intersection of quantum information theory and computational physics, and the condition number saturation result is of fundamental interest for understanding the complexity of quantum linear solvers. This paper provides a concrete example of quantum advantage in a practical domain, which is a key area of research in quantum physics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper is a valuable contribution to the field of quantum computing applied to computational electromagnetics. It provides a rigorous benchmarking of two prominent quantum algorithms on realistic FDTD problems and uncovers a crucial scaling property (condition number saturation) that enhances the feasibility of quantum solvers. The results are promising, but the lack of hardware implementation and detailed resource estimates limits the immediate practical impact. Nevertheless, the work is novel and well-executed, and it opens up new avenues for research in quantum algorithms for PDEs. It is likely to be of interest to both quantum computing researchers and computational physicists.

tldr: This paper studies trapping and caging in Sokoban-type models, where a random walker pushes obstacles, focusing on the statistics of trapping times and the role of obstacle pushing in disordered media.
motivation: Understanding how obstacles and pushing affect the motion of a random walker in disordered media is relevant to transport and diffusion in complex environments, which connects to thermodynamic and stochastic processes.
method: The authors analyze one-dimensional Sokoban models with arbitrary pushing capacity, deriving exact results for trapping times and related quantities using random walk theory and disorder averaging.
result: They find that the ability to push obstacles significantly alters the trapping statistics, leading to anomalous diffusion and non-trivial dependence on obstacle density and pushing capacity.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the interplay between disorder and active pushing in stochastic transport, with implications for understanding diffusion in crowded or disordered systems.

authors: Rupak Majumder, Anish Acharya, And Shamik Gupta

Stochastic resetting has emerged as a powerful mechanism for driving systems into nonequilibrium stationary states with tunable properties. While most existing studies focus on global resetting, where all degrees of freedom are simultaneously reset, recent work has shown that resetting only a subset…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 024108] Published Wed Aug 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper analytically studies the effect of resetting only a subset of oscillators in generalized Kuramoto models, showing that such subsystem resetting can lead to nontrivial stationary states and synchronization transitions.
motivation: Stochastic resetting is a known mechanism to drive systems into nonequilibrium stationary states, but most studies consider global resetting. The authors aim to understand the effect of resetting only a subset of degrees of freedom, which is more realistic and can lead to richer dynamics.
method: They develop an analytical approach for generalized Kuramoto models with subsystem resetting, deriving equations for the order parameter and stationary distributions, and analyze the synchronization transition.
result: They find that subsystem resetting can induce synchronization even when the coupling is below the critical value for the original model, and the stationary state depends on the resetting rate and the fraction of reset oscillators.
conclusion: Subsystem resetting provides a new control mechanism for synchronization in oscillator systems, with potential applications in controlling collective behavior.

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:

Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) serve as important examples of ergodicity-breaking phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. In this paper, we study a two-dimensional quantum [MATH] gauge model that is dual to a two-dimensional spin-[MATH] XY model defined on bipartite graphs. We identify the exact eigenstates of the XY model with a tower structure as exact QMBS. Exploiting the duality transformation, we show that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) after the transformation are the exact QMBS of the dual [MATH] gauge model. This construction is versatile and has potential applications for finding new QMBS in other higher-dimensional models.

.
tldr: This paper constructs exact quantum many-body scars in a 2D quantum gauge model via duality to an XY model, providing a new example of ergodicity breaking in higher dimensions.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars are rare in dimensions higher than one, and this work aims to find exact QMBS in 2D gauge models, which are relevant to quantum thermodynamics and thermalization.
method: The authors study a 2D quantum gauge model dual to a spin-1/2 XY model on bipartite graphs, identify exact eigenstates with a tower structure in the XY model, and use duality to map them to QMBS in the gauge model.
result: They demonstrate that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) become exact QMBS of the dual gauge model, providing a versatile construction for finding QMBS in higher-dimensional models.
conclusion: This work expands the known examples of exact QMBS to 2D gauge theories, potentially impacting the understanding of thermalization and ergodicity breaking in quantum many-body systems.

title: Spin-based True Random Number Generation Enabled By Voltage-amplified Quantum Fluctuations
authors: Jie Zheng, Jiyong Kang, Zheng Zhu, Di Wu, Yuesheng Li, Dongxing Yu, Jiayong Wang, Hongxing Xu And Chenglong Jia
abstract: We investigate spin quantum-fluctuation effects that originate from the Heisenberg uncertainty principle during the dynamical cycle of disentanglement, entanglement, and re-disentanglement between itinerant electrons and localized magnetic moments mediated by the s–d exchange interaction. Beyond conventional deterministic spin-transfer torque, we analyze an intrinsic mechanism that transfers spin quantum fluctuations to a nanomagnet. By extending the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation to incorporate both quantum and thermal stochastic fields, we identify a temperature regime in which quantum fluctuations dominate the magnetization dynamics. We further show that voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy exponentially amplifies spin quantum fluctuations, enabling binary readout through magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions. These findings provide a microscopic framework for fluctuation-driven spin dynamics and outline a device-level pathway toward spin-based quantum true random number generation.
tldr: This paper proposes a device-level mechanism for spin-based true random number generation by exploiting voltage-amplified spin quantum fluctuations in magnetic tunnel junctions.
motivation: To provide a microscopic framework for fluctuation-driven spin dynamics and a pathway to quantum true random number generation using spintronic devices.
method: Extends the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation to include quantum and thermal stochastic fields, and analyzes the effect of voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy on spin quantum fluctuations.
result: Identifies a temperature regime where quantum fluctuations dominate, and shows that voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy exponentially amplifies these fluctuations, enabling binary readout via magnetoresistance.
conclusion: The findings offer a device-level approach to spin-based quantum random number generation, but the work is more applied and device-oriented, with limited direct connection to the core hybrid quantum systems topics.
