title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review covers tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution, a technique in nanoscale optical imaging.
motivation: To provide an overview of a scanning probe technique that combines optical fluorescence with atomic resolution, useful for studying molecules and their reactions.
method: The paper is a review article summarizing the principles and recent advances in tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy, including the use of a scanning tip as a nanoscale optical antenna.
result: The technique achieves superresolution down to the atomic scale, enabling the study of electronic and vibronic properties of individual molecules.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy is a powerful tool for nanoscale imaging and spectroscopy, with potential applications in molecular identification and reaction studies.

title: A Generalized K -space Coherent Averaging Method For Engineering Lattices Of Spin–orbit B...
authors: Pinki Chahal, Naume Shentevski, Priyanka Vadnere, David G Cory, Owen Lailey, Dmitry A Pushin And Dusan Sarenac
abstract: Spin–orbit beams, in which the orbital angular momentum degree of freedom is coupled to a two-level system such as polarization of light or spin in electrons and neutrons, have gained significant interest for their unique propagation properties and potential applications in imaging, material characterization, optical trapping, and quantum information processing. In this work we introduce a method for generating and engineering two-dimensional lattices of such spin–orbit beams based on coherent averaging in -space. By programming the angle, amplitude, and polarization of a set of input beams we obtain precise control over lattice geometry and period, as well as the orbital and radial degrees of freedom inside each unit cell. We explore both electromagnetic and matter wave implementations, and we experimentally demonstrate the generation and characterization of a micron-scale optical hexagonal lattice with well defined orbital and radial numbers in each unit cell. The described methods provide a robust and general method of generating and controlling structured waves such as optical skyrmions and matter wave implementations of orbit and spin–orbit beams.
tldr: This paper introduces a method for generating two-dimensional lattices of spin-orbit beams using coherent averaging in k-space, with experimental demonstration in optics.
motivation: To provide a robust and general method for generating and controlling structured waves such as optical skyrmions and matter wave implementations of spin-orbit beams, which have applications in imaging, material characterization, and quantum information processing.
method: The method programs the angle, amplitude, and polarization of input beams to achieve precise control over lattice geometry and period, as well as orbital and radial degrees of freedom inside each unit cell. Both electromagnetic and matter wave implementations are explored.
result: Experimental demonstration of a micron-scale optical hexagonal lattice with well-defined orbital and radial numbers in each unit cell.
conclusion: The described methods provide a robust and general approach for generating and controlling structured waves, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Observation Of Node-dependent Rydberg Molecular Bound States
authors: Qing Li, Shi-Yao Shao, Jun Zhang, Han-Chao Chen, Li-Hua Zhang, Bang Liu, Guang-Can Guo, Dong-Sheng Ding, Bao-Sen Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.09950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultralong-range Rydberg molecules, formed by the interaction between a highly excited Rydberg atom and a ground-state atom, provide a unique platform for exploring quantum phenomena spanning nanometer-to-micrometer distances as well as exotic few-body interactions. The formation mechanisms and resultant physical properties differ markedly between s-wave and p-wave scattering channels. Here we report the experimental observation of node-dependent p-wave molecular signals in Rb(nS)-Rb(5S) Rydberg molecular spectra, where variations in the principal quantum number n directly reveal the shift of molecular binding energies induced by the moving nodal structure of the Rydberg electron wavefunction. This node-dependence is attributed to a cooperative effect between the local gradient of the nS-electron wavefunction and the energydependent p-wave scattering length. In addition, resolving two p-wave bound states associated with adjacent nodes highlights the remarkable sub-nanometer spatial resolution achieved in our experiment. Our findings reveal a more profound quantum control mechanism, wherein the principal quantum number acts as a switch for nodal-selective molecular bound states, and the reported method provides a sensitive spectroscopic probe of electron-atom scattering.
tldr: This paper reports experimental observation of node-dependent p-wave Rydberg molecular bound states in Rb(nS)-Rb(5S) spectra, revealing quantum control via principal quantum number.
motivation: To explore ultralong-range Rydberg molecules and understand how the nodal structure of the Rydberg electron wavefunction affects molecular binding energies, providing a sensitive probe of electron-atom scattering.
method: Spectroscopic measurements of Rb(nS)-Rb(5S) Rydberg molecular spectra for varying principal quantum numbers n, resolving p-wave bound states associated with adjacent nodes.
result: Observation of node-dependent p-wave molecular signals, with shifts in binding energies correlated with the moving nodal structure, and resolution of two p-wave bound states demonstrating sub-nanometer spatial resolution.
conclusion: The principal quantum number acts as a switch for nodal-selective molecular bound states, offering a new quantum control mechanism and a sensitive spectroscopic probe.

title: Degenerate High-order Hybrid Bound States In The Continuum Beyond Diffraction Limit
authors: Nicolae C. Panoiu Ji Tong Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate the existence of at-[MATH] degenerate hybrid bound-states in the continuum (BICs) with high-order topological charges and quadratic band degeneracy in periodic photonic structures with [MATH] symmetry above the diffraction limit. The degenerate BICs are realized by combining symmetry protection, which suppresses radiation into zeroth-order diffraction channel, with quadratic band degeneracy and parameter tuning to eliminate radiation into first-order diffraction channels. An effective Hamiltonian is used to investigate the band structure around the degeneracy point, and the topological dynamics in all diffraction channels are characterized. This work reveals a novel mechanism for realizing degenerate BICs above the diffraction limit, opening up opportunities for new physics and applications.
tldr: This paper demonstrates degenerate high-order hybrid bound states in the continuum (BICs) in periodic photonic structures with C4 symmetry above the diffraction limit.
motivation: The authors aim to realize degenerate BICs with high-order topological charges and quadratic band degeneracy, which could enable new physics and applications in photonics.
method: They combine symmetry protection to suppress radiation into zeroth-order diffraction, and use quadratic band degeneracy and parameter tuning to eliminate radiation into first-order diffraction channels. An effective Hamiltonian is used to analyze the band structure and topological dynamics.
result: They demonstrate the existence of degenerate hybrid BICs with high-order topological charges and quadratic band degeneracy above the diffraction limit.
conclusion: This work reveals a novel mechanism for realizing degenerate BICs above the diffraction limit, opening opportunities for new physics and applications.

title: Active Electronic Terahertz Imaging For Industrial Applications: From Hardware To The Paradigm Shift By Artificial Intelligence
authors: Aparajita Bandyopadhyay, Hui Yuan, Willie J. Padilla, David J. Brady, Hartmut G. Roskos
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Imaging with terahertz (THz) radiation (0.3-10 THz) benefits from a unique combination of attributes: penetration through dry, non-polar packaging materials; variations of dielectric functions to provide contrast; the existence of spectral fingerprint resonances for some classes of materials; non-ionizing photon energies that are safe for use around humans; and - viewed from the low-frequency side - an extension of the capabilities of microwave radar to higher frequencies and thus to substantially better spatial resolution, at wavelengths which still permit direct measurement of the complex-valued radiation field. This review concentrates on active THz imaging with electronic sources combined with power detectors or coherent receivers - the system class most likely to deliver fast (ideally real-time), cost-effective and deployable solutions for a wide range of industrial applications such as quality control, non-destructive testing, security screening and ranging for situational awareness. Such systems should be deployable on robotic and emerging autonomous platforms. We review the state of the art of compact semiconductor detector arrays, of imaging modalities ranging from focused-beam raster and frequency-modulated continuous-wave architectures to coherent Fourier-plane acquisition, and of augmentation techniques such as compressive sensing. Particular attention is paid to the growing role of artificial intelligence: from convolutional neural networks and physics-informed deep learning for phase retrieval and image reconstruction, to agentic frameworks for autonomous system design. The bottlenecks of THz imaging - acquisition speed, resolution, contrast and cost - are re-examined in the light of these innovations, and a reference-anchored technology roadmap is derived which projects an order-of-magnitude reduction in the measurement requirements of THz imaging.
tldr: This paper reviews active electronic terahertz imaging for industrial applications, focusing on hardware and AI-based techniques.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a comprehensive overview of THz imaging systems and their potential for industrial deployment, addressing bottlenecks like speed, resolution, and cost.
method: The review covers compact semiconductor detector arrays, various imaging modalities (raster, FMCW, coherent Fourier-plane), and augmentation techniques like compressive sensing, with emphasis on AI methods such as CNNs and physics-informed deep learning.
result: The paper derives a technology roadmap projecting an order-of-magnitude reduction in measurement requirements for THz imaging.
conclusion: Active THz imaging with electronic sources and AI integration is poised for significant advances, enabling fast and cost-effective industrial applications.

title: What Should A Linear Optical Frontend Compute? Assessing The Role Of Meta-optics, Nonlocality, And Coherence In Hybrid Inference Systems
authors: Nicholas Behrens, Yandong Li, Francesco Monticone
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid inference systems that pair an optical frontend with a digital backend offer a route to offload computation to the physical layer. Yet what the optics should compute, and when this is beneficial, has remained unclear. Here, we show that, for classification tasks, a well-designed optical frontend reshapes the statistics of the sensor intensity readout to improve class separability, quantified by the Bhattacharyya distance. This training-free metric predicts downstream accuracy and reveals that much of the discriminative information resides in inter-pixel correlations. We then identify the roles of coherence and different forms of nonlocality. Because the sensor measures intensity, a linear frontend produces features that are quadratic in the input field; however, only nonlocal, coherent optical systems can exploit the associated information. Such systems can yield significant performance gains, surpassing the best trained linear preprocessor. These results provide physical insights and new design principles for optimal optical--electronic inference systems.
tldr: This paper analyzes the role of optical frontends in hybrid inference systems, showing that nonlocal coherent optics can improve classification by exploiting inter-pixel correlations.
motivation: To clarify what an optical frontend should compute in hybrid optical-electronic inference systems and when such computation is beneficial.
method: The authors use the Bhattacharyya distance as a training-free metric to quantify class separability, and analyze the roles of coherence and nonlocality in linear optical frontends.
result: They find that nonlocal, coherent optical systems can exploit quadratic features in the intensity readout, yielding performance gains over trained linear preprocessors.
conclusion: The work provides design principles for optimal optical-electronic inference systems, highlighting the importance of coherence and nonlocality.

title: Equilibrium Distributions For Strongly Nonlinear Many-Body Systems
authors: Jialin Zhang, Yong Zhang, Hong Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Obtaining equilibrium distributions of nonlinear systems is essential for accurately computing macroscopic observables. Conventional theoretical corrections are typically limited to weak nonlinearities, where interaction terms can be treated as effectively uncorrelated perturbations and the random phase approximation applies. In this Letter, we develop a framework to determine equilibrium distributions based on the generalized energy equipartition principle. Our approach recovers existing corrections in the weakly nonlinear regime and, crucially, remains valid for strong nonlinearities, where perturbative contributions become correlated and conventional approaches break down. Numerical simulations of the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation, the Majda-McLaughlin-Tabak model, and the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou model demonstrate accurate corrections for nonlinearities more than an order of magnitude stronger than those accessible to conventional theories.
tldr: This paper develops a framework for computing equilibrium distributions in strongly nonlinear many-body systems using generalized energy equipartition, validated on several nonlinear models.
motivation: Conventional theoretical corrections for equilibrium distributions fail for strong nonlinearities due to correlated perturbations, limiting accurate macroscopic observable computation.
method: The authors propose a framework based on the generalized energy equipartition principle that remains valid for strong nonlinearities, and test it via numerical simulations on the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, Majda-McLaughlin-Tabak model, and Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou model.
result: The framework accurately corrects equilibrium distributions for nonlinearities more than an order of magnitude stronger than those accessible to conventional theories.
conclusion: The work provides a robust method for determining equilibrium distributions in strongly nonlinear systems, extending beyond weak nonlinearity limits.

title: Outdoor 100-m-scale Air Waveguides
authors: Andrew Goffin, Gregory Babic, Andrew Derusha, Maksim Livshits, Howard Milchberg, Patrick Skrodzki
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical power densities for standoff spectroscopy, remote sensing, directed energy, and free-space optical communications are limited by diffraction and adverse atmospheric conditions such as turbulence, fog, and wind. Air waveguides, generated by ultrashort-pulsed laser filamentation, are a promising approach for transmission and collection of optical signals over long distances, overcoming beam diffraction and, for point-like sources, inverse square signal falloff with distance. In this work, we demonstrate outdoor guiding for the first time over a record length of ~100 m, exceeding the prior (indoor) record of 42 m. We correlate air waveguide performance to a range of real atmospheric conditions including turbulent refractive index structure parameter ([MATH]) values up to ~[MATH], crosswind speeds up to ~2 m/s, as well as temperature, pressure, and humidity variations. Accompanying propagation simulations provide insight into the real effects of these environmental perturbations, particularly crosswind, on waveguide performance and lifetime. Our results pave the way for quasi-continuous air waveguiding with kHz-scale repetition rate filaments in challenging outdoor environments.
tldr: This paper demonstrates outdoor air waveguides over ~100 m using laser filamentation, a record length, and studies the effects of atmospheric conditions on performance.
motivation: Air waveguides could enable long-distance optical transmission and collection, overcoming diffraction and atmospheric disturbances, but previous demonstrations were limited to indoor settings.
method: The authors generated air waveguides via ultrashort-pulsed laser filamentation and measured their performance over ~100 m outdoors, correlating with atmospheric parameters and using simulations to understand environmental effects.
result: They achieved a record outdoor guiding length of ~100 m, exceeding the previous indoor record of 42 m, and characterized performance under turbulence, crosswind, and other conditions.
conclusion: The results suggest that quasi-continuous air waveguiding with kHz-scale repetition rate filaments is feasible in challenging outdoor environments, paving the way for practical applications.

title: Causality Sum Rules In Conventional Scattering Matrices
authors: Ning Han, Rui Zhao, Shuxing Yang, Mingzhu Li, Hongsheng Chen, Yihao Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scattering matrices are the standard experimental and computational description of photonic and electromagnetic devices. Passivity is explicit in the conventional incoming-outgoing matrix, whereas causality sum rules are usually formulated only after transforming the response into auxiliary variables. Here we show that these rules can be written directly in the conventional scattering matrix by removing the time advance introduced by the reference domain. Using the earliest-arrival delay of each channel, we define a domain-delayed matrix that preserves real-frequency passivity while restoring the causal time origin. Under explicit analyticity, transparency, and regularity assumptions, this matrix becomes a Schur function, enabling a Cayley-Herglotz construction. The resulting projected and determinant bounds constrain coherent channel superpositions and aggregate multichannel loss. The framework recovers Rozanov's absorber limit and spherical-multipole sum rules, while extending causality bounds to measurable quantities including insertion loss, suppressed singular-value channels, and conditional lossless delay-bandwidth trade-offs. Our work directly connects fundamental causality theory with experimentally accessible scattering data. The initial theoretical route is autonomously explored by Qiushi Engine, an AI research system for open-ended scientific discovery, and subsequently verified, refined, and developed by the authors, demonstrating a hybrid AI-human discovery workflow.
tldr: This paper derives causality sum rules directly in conventional scattering matrices for photonic devices, connecting fundamental causality theory with measurable scattering data.
motivation: Causality sum rules are typically formulated in auxiliary variables, not directly in the conventional scattering matrix, limiting their direct application to experimental data.
method: The authors define a domain-delayed matrix by removing time advances from the reference domain, preserving passivity and restoring causal time origin, then use analyticity and transparency assumptions to construct a Schur function via Cayley-Herglotz.
result: They obtain projected and determinant bounds constraining coherent channel superpositions and multichannel loss, recovering Rozanov's absorber limit and spherical-multipole sum rules, and extending to insertion loss and delay-bandwidth trade-offs.
conclusion: The work provides a direct bridge between causality theory and experimentally accessible scattering data, with potential applications in photonic device design.

title: 730-nm Optical Parametric Conversion From Near- To Short-wave Infrared Band
authors: J. M. Chavez Boggio, J. R. Windmiller, M. Knutzen, R. Jiang, C. Bres, N. Alic, B. Stossel, K. Rottwitt, S. Radic
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A record 730 nm parametric conversion in silica fiber from the near-infrared to the short-wave infrared band is reported and analyzed. A parametric gain in excess of 30 dB was measured for a signal at 1300 nm (with corresponding idler at 2030 nm). This conversion was performed in a travelling single-pass one-pump parametric architecture and high efficiency is achieved by a combination of high peak power and a nonlinear fiber with a reduced fourth-order dispersion coefficient.
tldr: This paper reports a record 730 nm parametric conversion in silica fiber from near-infrared to short-wave infrared, achieving >30 dB gain.
motivation: The work aims to extend the wavelength range of fiber-based parametric converters for applications in optical communications and sensing.
method: The authors use a single-pass one-pump parametric architecture with high peak power and a nonlinear fiber engineered to have reduced fourth-order dispersion.
result: They demonstrate a parametric gain exceeding 30 dB for a signal at 1300 nm with idler at 2030 nm, achieving a record conversion span of 730 nm.
conclusion: The results show that careful dispersion engineering enables broad wavelength conversion in silica fibers, which could be useful for various photonic applications.

title: Unified Exact Cylindrical Dirac Modes And Symmetry-Resolved Quantum Geometry
authors: Zhongze Guo, Bei Xu, Qiang Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact cylindrical solutions of the free Dirac equation provide natural single-particle modes for a broad class of axially symmetric relativistic fermion systems, including electron vortices, twisted-particle scattering, rotating matter, and cylindrical field quantization, but are commonly formulated in different internal bases. We derive the general regular positive-energy cylindrical solution at fixed energy, transverse and longitudinal momenta, and total angular momentum, and show how the commonly used spin-polarized, separation, helicity, and transverse-helicity modes are embedded in the resulting two-dimensional solution space. A conserved transverse operator resolves the residual doublet into two symmetry-defined branches. Their parameter-dependent eigenspaces admit a gauge-invariant quantum-geometric characterization, with opposite Berry curvatures, a common quantum metric, and saturation of the two-level metric--curvature relation. We further derive symmetry constraints on branch conversion and the corresponding reduced two-state dynamics. The resulting framework connects mode classification, symmetry resolution, quantum geometry, and dynamics across distinct cylindrical Dirac settings.
tldr: This paper derives exact cylindrical solutions of the Dirac equation and analyzes their quantum geometry, but it is not related to the user's research interests.
motivation: The paper aims to unify various cylindrical Dirac modes and characterize their symmetry-resolved quantum geometry, which is a topic in mathematical physics and quantum mechanics.
method: The authors derive general regular positive-energy cylindrical solutions and show how common modes are embedded, then use a conserved transverse operator to resolve the doublet and compute Berry curvature and quantum metric.
result: They find opposite Berry curvatures, a common quantum metric, and saturation of the metric-curvature relation, along with symmetry constraints on branch conversion.
conclusion: The framework connects mode classification, symmetry resolution, quantum geometry, and dynamics in cylindrical Dirac systems, but it is not relevant to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Stability Of Orbital Angular Momentum Modes In Conventional And Ring-Core Optical Fibers
authors: Hassan Asgharzadeh B., Regina Gumenyuk, Marco Ornigotti
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modal dynamics in multimode optical fibers are fundamentally governed by the inter- play between phase matching and intermodal coupling. In this work, we investigate the fundamental coupling mechanisms in ring-core fibers and identify a geometry-induced cou- pling suppression that significantly reduces coupling coefficients between orbital angular momentum modes compared to conventional multimode step-index fibers. This mechanism provides a clear physical explanation for the superior transmission stability of orbital angular momentum modes in ring-core fibers and establishes specific geometric constraints for the design of ring-core fiber-based mode converters.
tldr: This paper studies the stability of orbital angular momentum modes in ring-core fibers, identifying a geometry-induced coupling suppression that explains their superior transmission stability.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the fundamental coupling mechanisms in multimode optical fibers, specifically why ring-core fibers provide better stability for OAM modes compared to conventional step-index fibers.
method: They theoretically investigate intermodal coupling in ring-core fibers, deriving coupling coefficients and identifying a geometry-induced suppression mechanism.
result: They find that ring-core fibers significantly reduce coupling coefficients between OAM modes due to geometry, providing a physical explanation for their stability and design constraints for mode converters.
conclusion: The work establishes geometric constraints for designing ring-core fiber-based mode converters, contributing to optical fiber technology but not directly to the user's research interests.

title: Reflection Positivity In Free Fermionic Theories
authors: Manfred Salmhofer Carl Handrack
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reflection positivity is one of the Osterwalder--Schrader axioms for Euclidean quantum field theory, ensuring that the reconstructed relativistic Hilbert space carries a positive-definite inner product. For free fermionic theories whose covariance is a real rational function of the Dirac operator, we prove that reflection positivity holds if and only if all poles are real, simple, and carry non-negative residues. We also explicitly show the failure of reflection positivity for covariances with exponential regulators.
tldr: This paper proves a necessary and sufficient condition for reflection positivity in free fermionic theories with rational covariances, showing it holds iff all poles are real, simple, and have non-negative residues.
motivation: Reflection positivity is a key axiom in Euclidean quantum field theory, ensuring a positive-definite Hilbert space after Wick rotation. The authors aim to characterize when free fermionic theories satisfy this property.
method: The authors analyze the covariance as a real rational function of the Dirac operator and derive conditions on its poles and residues. They also examine covariances with exponential regulators to demonstrate failure.
result: They prove that reflection positivity holds if and only if all poles are real, simple, and carry non-negative residues, and explicitly show failure for exponential regulators.
conclusion: The work provides a clear criterion for reflection positivity in free fermionic theories, which is relevant to mathematical physics but not directly connected to the user's research directions.

title: Continuous-Time Covariance Steering With Common Free-Final Time: Finite-Horizon Solutions And Infinite-Horizon Limits
authors: Akan Selim, Fengjiao Liu, Siddhartha Ganguly, Panagiotis Tsiotras
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article studies the optimal common free-final time problem for steering the state covariance of a continuous-time stochastic linear system between prescribed initial and terminal covariance matrices. We first establish a deterministic reformulation of the SDE-constrained free-final time stochastic optimal control problem (SOCP). For the ensuing SOCP, we provide necessary conditions for optimality and establish sufficient conditions for the optimal common final time to be finite. Subsequently, we characterize the asymptotic behavior of the finite-horizon optimal solutions as the final time tends to infinity, the invariant sets and trajectories associated with this limiting regime, and derive the sensitivity of the Hamiltonian with respect to the common final time. Finally, leveraging these sensitivities, we develop a trust-region line-search algorithm together with an infinite-horizon case detection method, and demonstrate its performance on three different problems: (a) an illustrative covariance-steering example, (b) a demonstration of spacecraft maneuver using covariance control, and (c) Gaussian mixture to Gaussian mixture steering.
tldr: This paper addresses optimal control of stochastic linear systems for covariance steering, which is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The paper aims to solve a free-final-time optimal control problem for steering the state covariance of a stochastic linear system, with applications in spacecraft maneuvers and Gaussian mixture steering.
method: The authors reformulate the SDE-constrained problem deterministically, derive necessary and sufficient conditions for optimality, analyze asymptotic behavior as final time tends to infinity, and develop a trust-region line-search algorithm with infinite-horizon detection.
result: They provide finite-horizon solutions, characterize infinite-horizon limits, and demonstrate the algorithm on three examples including spacecraft maneuver and Gaussian mixture steering.
conclusion: The paper contributes to control theory and stochastic optimal control, but has no connection to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Kullback-Leibler Mirror-Prox For Measure-Valued Variational Inequalities And Mean-Field Equilibria
authors: Erhan Bayraktar, Ibrahim Ekren, Lu Vy, Ziqing Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the computation of static mean-field equilibria on a compact state space by formulating the equilibrium condition as a variational inequality over probability measures. We propose an entropic variant of Korpelevich's extragradient algorithm---the Kullback--Leibler Mirror-Prox method---in which Euclidean projections are replaced by relative-entropy proximal steps. Each half-step is therefore an explicit exponential reweighting of the current measure, implemented on a finite state-space discretization. Under Lasry--Lions monotonicity and continuity assumptions, we prove convergence of mesh-refined ergodic averages and obtain finite-iteration Minty-residual and approximate-equilibrium bounds that jointly quantify iteration and discretization errors. Under strong monotonicity, we derive metric convergence rates for the last, best, and averaged iterates. We also develop a KL-type Tikhonov regularization that selects the equilibrium minimizing relative entropy with respect to a reference measure. The framework applies to potential and nonpotential cost operators and does not require differentiability or convexity of the cost in the individual state.
tldr: This paper proposes a Kullback-Leibler Mirror-Prox algorithm for computing mean-field equilibria via variational inequalities over probability measures.
motivation: The authors aim to compute static mean-field equilibria on compact state spaces, which is a problem in game theory and optimization, not directly related to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: They formulate the equilibrium condition as a variational inequality and introduce an entropic variant of Korpelevich's extragradient algorithm, using relative-entropy proximal steps and exponential reweighting on a discretized state space.
result: They prove convergence of mesh-refined ergodic averages and obtain finite-iteration bounds under monotonicity, plus metric convergence rates under strong monotonicity, and develop a KL-type Tikhonov regularization.
conclusion: The framework provides a computational method for mean-field equilibria with theoretical guarantees, but it is outside the scope of the user's research interests.

title: Efficient Weak-Entropy Pinn For Solving Hyperbolic Conservation Laws
authors: Qi Gao, Kuang Huang, Xuan Di
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, neural networks have significantly advanced numerical solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs). However, solving PDEs with discontinuous solutions, such as hyperbolic conservation laws, remains challenging for neural network-based methods such as physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). Existing methods often rely on strong prior assumptions such as knowledge of discontinuity locations, or they introduce artificial smoothing terms that degrade accuracy. However, accurately solving these conservation laws and predicting the formation and propagation of discontinuities in solutions is crucial in many practical applications, including gas dynamics and traffic flow modeling. In this paper, we introduce a novel Weak-Entropy PINN (WEPINN) framework for hyperbolic conservation laws with discontinuous solutions. The method enforces the governing equations in their weak (integral) formulation and incorporates the entropy condition to select the physically admissible solution, while employing the discrete fast Fourier transform (DFFT) for efficient numerical integration. Our method is tested through extensive numerical experiments on a variety of scalar conservation laws and systems of conservation laws in one and two dimensional spaces. These experiments demonstrate that our method can accurately resolve sharp discontinuities while effectively capturing interactions between multiple shock and rarefaction waves.
tldr: This paper introduces a Weak-Entropy PINN framework for solving hyperbolic conservation laws with discontinuous solutions.
motivation: Neural network methods like PINNs struggle with discontinuous solutions of hyperbolic conservation laws, often requiring prior knowledge of discontinuities or introducing artificial smoothing.
method: The proposed WEPINN enforces the weak (integral) form of the governing equations and incorporates the entropy condition to select physically admissible solutions, using discrete fast Fourier transform for efficient integration.
result: Extensive numerical experiments on scalar and systems of conservation laws in 1D and 2D show accurate resolution of sharp discontinuities and capture of shock and rarefaction wave interactions.
conclusion: The method provides an efficient and accurate approach for solving hyperbolic conservation laws with discontinuities using neural networks.

title: Exponentially Consistent Low Complexity Tests For Statistical Sequence Matching
authors: Lin Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Towards practical applications of statistical sequence matching, we propose low complexity tests that are exponentially consistent and bound the exponential decay rates for error probabilities of our proposed tests. In statistical sequence matching, one is given two databases of multiple sequences, where in each database, each sequence is generated i.i.d. from a distinct distribution. A pair of sequences, one from each database, is said matched if they are generated from the same distribution. The number of matched pairs of sequences, a.k.a, the number of matches, can be either zero or positive. We consider both cases of known and unknown number of matches. When the number of matches is known and positive, the task is to identify all matched pairs of sequences. To construct fixed-length tests, we calculate the scoring function values for all pairs of sequences across the two databases and identify the matched pairs as those having small enough pairwise scoring function values. We show that our proposed test is exponentially consistent, which strikes a better tradeoff between complexity and performance than existing fixed-length tests that use exhaustive search. To construct sequential tests, we need an additional positive threshold to determine the stopping time, and we show that our sequential test achieves strictly better performance than our fixed-length test. Subsequently, we generalize our results to the case with unknown number of matches.
tldr: This paper proposes low-complexity tests for statistical sequence matching with exponential consistency, but it is a classical information theory problem with no quantum component.
motivation: The paper aims to make statistical sequence matching practical by reducing computational complexity while maintaining exponential error decay.
method: The authors design fixed-length and sequential tests based on pairwise scoring functions, analyzing their error exponents and complexity tradeoffs.
result: The proposed tests are exponentially consistent and achieve better complexity-performance tradeoffs than exhaustive search, with sequential tests outperforming fixed-length tests.
conclusion: The work contributes to classical statistical inference but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Entropy Scales In Topological Dynamical Systems
authors: Yunxiang Xie, Ercai Chen, Xiaoyao Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by Helfter's notion of scaling, we introduce Bowen entropy scales and local measure-theoretic counterparts associated with general scaling families. Under a controlled decay condition, we establish a variational principle on compact subsets using Billingsley-type and Frostman-type arguments. We also define entropy and pressure scales via separated sets and prove an abstract variational principle using convex duality. The framework recovers classical entropy and includes examples related to slow entropy and entropy dimension. For the induced system, we give sufficient conditions under which the original system has zero upper capacity entropy scale if and only if the induced system does. Under a further condition on the scaling family, we prove that a positive upper capacity entropy scale of the original system implies an infinite upper capacity entropy scale of the induced system. We also provide a full-shift example showing that this conclusion does not hold for arbitrary scaling families. Finally, we define upper capacity entropy scales along prescribed increasing sequences of times and prove the corresponding zero-entropy result for induced systems.
tldr: This paper introduces entropy scales for topological dynamical systems, generalizing classical entropy via scaling families and proving variational principles.
motivation: To extend entropy theory to systems with sub-exponential or non-standard growth rates, motivated by Helfter's scaling notion.
method: Defines Bowen entropy scales and local measure-theoretic counterparts, uses Billingsley-type and Frostman-type arguments, and convex duality for variational principles.
result: Establishes variational principles for compact subsets and abstract entropy/pressure scales, recovers classical entropy, and provides conditions for induced systems.
conclusion: Provides a general framework for entropy scales, with applications to slow entropy and entropy dimension, but is purely mathematical and not connected to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Secure Cooperative THz Isac Via Mamba Empowered Graph Neural Network Precoding
authors: Chao Wang, Zan Li, Xiangnan Zhou, Haibin Zhang, Hao Xu, Liang Jin, Derrick Wing Kwan Ng
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The terahertz (THz) band offers abundant spectrum resources for high-throughput communication and ultra high-precision localization. This paper investigates secure communication in cooperative THz orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) bistatic integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) systems, where multiple base stations (BSs) equipped with extremely large-scale antenna arrays (ELAAs) collaboratively serve downlink users while concurrently locating multiple targets. Malicious targets are assumed to act as potential eavesdroppers attempting to intercept confidential information intended for legitimate users. To mitigate these threats, we formulate a joint optimization problem for analog beamforming, digital precoding, true-time delayers (TTDs), and sensing signal covariance matrix design. The objective is to maximize the minimum secrecy rate subject to Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) constraints that ensure localization accuracy. This problem is highly challenging due to the non-convex CRB constraint, strongly coupled variables, high computational complexity from ELAA, and near-field channel modeling. To address these challenges, we propose a novel data-driven framework that integrates graph neural networks (GNNs) with the Mamba architecture. Our proposed framework first encodes the interactions among users, targets, and BSs into a heterogeneous graph and then employs message passing to optimize vertex features. The Mamba blocks further enhance this process through their selection mechanism and state space modeling capabilities, enabling dynamic and context-aware optimization of beamforming, TTD configurations, and sensing parameters. Numerical simulations validate that the proposed method outperforms both conventional and learning-based baselines, while offering high computational efficiency and strong generalization across different network conditions.
tldr: This paper proposes a GNN-Mamba framework for secure beamforming in THz ISAC systems, focusing on physical-layer security and localization.
motivation: The paper addresses secure communication in THz ISAC systems with malicious eavesdroppers, aiming to maximize secrecy rate while ensuring localization accuracy.
method: It formulates a joint optimization problem for beamforming, TTDs, and sensing covariance, and solves it with a data-driven GNN-Mamba architecture that encodes interactions in a heterogeneous graph.
result: Numerical simulations show the proposed method outperforms conventional and learning-based baselines in secrecy rate, computational efficiency, and generalization.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the potential of graph neural networks and Mamba for secure ISAC, but it is primarily an applied engineering contribution without deep information-theoretic or thermodynamic insights.

title: On $\ell$-rank Additive Intersection Pairs (raip) Of Codes
authors: Sanjit Bhowmick, Kuntal Deka, Sihem Mesnager
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces and studies \(\ell\)-rank additive intersection pairs (RAIP) of codes over finite fields for a given positive integer \(\ell\). The notion of \(\ell\)-RAIP provides a common framework that generalizes additive complementary dual (ACD) codes, additive complementary pairs (ACP) of codes, and the hull of an additive code. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions characterizing when a pair of additive codes forms an \(\ell\)-RAIP. Furthermore, for (q>2), we prove that any pair of additive codes is monomially equivalent to an ACP of codes. As a consequence, for (q>3), every additive code is monomially equivalent to an ACD code. { A key contribution of the paper is a general construction method for \(\ell\)-RAIP of codes derived from self-orthogonal additive codes, which yields families of \((\ell+1)\)-RAIP of codes under suitable conditions.} In addition, several explicit constructions of \(\ell\)-RAIP of codes are presented.
tldr: This paper introduces and studies ℓ-rank additive intersection pairs (RAIP) of codes over finite fields, generalizing ACD codes, ACP codes, and hulls, with constructions and equivalence results.
motivation: The authors aim to unify and generalize existing notions of complementary and hull codes within a common framework, potentially useful for coding theory and cryptography.
method: They define ℓ-RAIP, characterize them via necessary and sufficient conditions, prove monomial equivalence results for q>2 and q>3, and provide constructions from self-orthogonal additive codes.
result: They establish conditions for ℓ-RAIP, show that any pair of additive codes is monomially equivalent to an ACP for q>2, and every additive code to an ACD for q>3, and construct families of (ℓ+1)-RAIP.
conclusion: The paper contributes to the theory of additive codes, but its focus is purely on algebraic coding theory without direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Successive Schur-Riesz Analysis For Approximation
authors: Matthew Francis Dixon
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many approximation methods enlarge a trial space by adjoining function blocks generated by different operators. Exact redundancy and strong cross-level interaction can make coefficients nonunique and render pairwise or diagonal-dominance tests needlessly pessimistic. For \(V_m=\sum_{\ell\leq m}S_\ell(E_\ell)\) in a Hilbert space [MATH], we quotient coefficients representing the same function and control successive orthogonal innovations to obtain Riesz bounds independent of \(m\). The setting includes factored operators \(S_\ell=T_\ell\circ\cdots\circ T_1:E_\ell\to\mathcal H\), with compatible intermediate spaces, but the theorem allows arbitrary bounded \(S_\ell\). The same constants control approximation, truncation, perturbation, and levelwise error. A block Schur complement identifies the intrinsic new dimension and gives the exact reduction in squared best-approximation error, leading to a constructive enrichment procedure. Nonstationary and lifted examples give positive intrinsic bounds where diagonal-dominance estimates are negative or labelled Gram matrices are singular; adaptive and recycled-subspace calculations illustrate the distinct roles of representation stability and application-specific utility.
tldr: This paper presents a mathematical framework for successive approximation in Hilbert spaces using Schur-Riesz analysis, focusing on redundancy and stability of coefficients.
motivation: To address nonuniqueness and pessimistic stability tests in approximation methods that enlarge trial spaces with function blocks from different operators.
method: The authors quotient coefficients representing the same function and control successive orthogonal innovations to derive Riesz bounds independent of the number of levels, using block Schur complements to identify intrinsic new dimensions.
result: They obtain uniform Riesz bounds and exact reductions in squared best-approximation error, with examples showing positive intrinsic bounds where diagonal-dominance tests fail.
conclusion: The proposed analysis provides a constructive enrichment procedure and clarifies the roles of representation stability and application-specific utility in approximation.

title: Polynomial Bounds On Degeneration Order From Commutativity Properties Of Tensor Slices
authors: Shree Ganesh, Pascal Koiran, Rafael Oliveira
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A tensor has border rank at most [MATH] if it can be written as [MATH] where [MATH] has rank at most [MATH] for all sufficiently small [MATH]. It is known that the map [MATH] can be assumed to be a (tensor valued) polynomial in [MATH]. The smallest possible degree of such a map is called the error degree of [MATH]. The error degree and the related notion of order of degeneration are the two key quantities that we study in this paper. One motivation comes from debordering: by polynomial interpolation on the map [MATH] we can upper bound the tensor rank of [MATH]. For order 3 tensors, exponential upper bounds on the error degree and degeneration order were given almost 40 years ago in (Lehmkuhl Lickteig, 1989) and were not improved ever since. In this paper we give bounds that apply to a wide class of tensors, exponentially improving on (Lehmkuhl Lickteig, 1989). Our results are most general for tensors with 3 slices (format [MATH]). In this case, our main assumption is on the rank of the matrix slices. We also give bounds that apply to arbitrary rectangular formats ([MATH]). In this case, we need an additional 1-regularity assumption on one of the slices of the tensor (recall that a matrix is said to be 1-regular if its eigenspaces are 1-dimensional). Under these assumptions we show that the error degree is at most 1, which yields a nontrivial debordering result (tensor rank at most [MATH] for border rank [MATH]). The results in (Lehmkuhl Lickteig, 1989) rely on an upper bound on the degree of the variety of tensors of border rank at most [MATH]. We rely instead on more specific properties of this algebraic variety, and in particular on commutativity properties of certain matrices derived from the tensor slices.

motivation: The authors aim to improve upon exponential bounds on error degree and degeneration order from 1989, motivated by debordering via polynomial interpolation.
method: They use algebraic geometry and commutativity properties of matrices derived from tensor slices to derive bounds on the degree of the variety of border rank tensors.
result: They obtain bounds that exponentially improve on previous results for a wide class of tensors, including error degree at most 1 under certain assumptions.
conclusion: The results provide new insights into the algebraic structure of tensor degeneration, potentially impacting complexity theory and algebraic algorithms.

title: Synthesizing Probabilistic Saturating Counters With Differentially Private Formal Guarantees
authors: Zhiming Chi, Lutan Zhao, Depeng Liu, Yong Li, Pengfei Yang, Bow-Yaw Wang, Rui Hou, Cheng-Chao Huang, Andrea Turrini, Lijun Zhang, Naijun Zhan
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Branch predictors improve instruction-level parallelism in modern processors and are commonly modeled using saturating counters. However, classical saturating counters are deterministic and thus vulnerable to side-channel attacks: an attacker can manipulate the counter state and infer the branch direction of a victim process. Probabilistic saturating counters (PSCs) have been proposed to mitigate this leakage by randomizing counter updates, but existing evaluations are mainly empirical. In this paper, we give a formal analysis based on differential privacy (DP): we model PSCs and the corresponding Prime+Probe attack strategies as probabilistic Moore machines, derive optimal attack strategies, and quantify the attacker's distinguishing power through DP. Our DP guarantee applies to the PSC primitive under the Prime+Probe observation model; end-to-end security for a full branch predictor under repeated or adaptive attacks is an important direction for future work. We then synthesize parameters for an enhanced PSC that satisfies a target pure DP guarantee. To evaluate utility, we derive the stationary misprediction rate and validate the theoretical predictions on benchmark programs. Compared to deterministic and existing probabilistic saturating counters, the synthesized PSCs provide formal security guarantees while preserving competitive prediction performance.
tldr: This paper formally analyzes probabilistic saturating counters in branch predictors using differential privacy, synthesizing parameters for security guarantees while maintaining prediction performance.
motivation: Classical saturating counters are vulnerable to side-channel attacks; probabilistic counters mitigate leakage but lack formal security guarantees.
method: The authors model PSCs and Prime+Probe attacks as probabilistic Moore machines, derive optimal attack strategies, quantify attacker distinguishing power via differential privacy, and synthesize parameters for a target DP guarantee.
result: The synthesized PSCs provide formal DP guarantees while achieving competitive misprediction rates on benchmarks compared to existing counters.
conclusion: The work offers a formal framework for designing secure branch predictors, though end-to-end security under repeated attacks remains future work.

title: A Lightweight Fault-Detection Scheme For Barrett Modular Multiplication Using Multiple Conditional Reduction Paths
authors: Rourab Paul, Paresh Baidya, Krishnendu Guha, Amlan Chakrabarti
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polynomial multiplication is the most resource-, time-, and energy-critical operation in lattice-based Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) schemes. Lattice-based PQC schemes such as Kyber and Dilithium have already been standardized, while lattice- based FHE schemes such as BGV, BFV, and CKKS are widely recognized as leading candidate in FHE area. Barrett Modular Multiplication (BMM) for polynomial multiplication is widely adopted in PQC and FHE hardware accelerators due to its hardware friendly nature and efficient modular reduction capabilities. However, Side-Channel Attacks (SCAs) and Hardware Trojans may introduce intentional faults, while aging and various other factors can cause unintentional faults. These faults may target the BM M unit, one of the most critical components of PQC and FHE infrastructures, potentially leading to information leakage and compromising system security. In this paper, we employ a Statistical Reduction Monitoring (SRM) method to protect the BM M unit against such adversarial conditions. The proposed approach incurs minimal hardware overhead while providing efficient detection of both random and bur.
tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight fault-detection scheme for Barrett modular multiplication in lattice-based cryptography, focusing on hardware security against side-channel attacks and hardware Trojans.
motivation: Faults in Barrett modular multiplication units can compromise the security of PQC and FHE systems, so efficient detection is needed.
method: The authors employ a Statistical Reduction Monitoring (SRM) method to detect random and burst faults with minimal hardware overhead.
result: The proposed scheme provides efficient detection of both random and burst faults with low hardware cost.
conclusion: The approach enhances the reliability and security of lattice-based cryptographic hardware without significant overhead.

title: A Consolidated Game Framework For Cooperative Defense Against Cross-Domain Cyber Attacks In Satellite-Enabled Internet Of Things
authors: Linan Huang, Peilong Liu, Xu Chen, Chunxiao Jiang, Linling Kuang, Jianhua Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the adoption of satellite-enabled Internet of Things (IoT) continues to rise, its intricate multidomain architecture becomes increasingly susceptible to cross-domain cyber threats. Attackers can exploit compromised IoT devices, inject malicious packets into data streams aggregated at the IoT gateway for satellite backhaul, and potentially endanger the satellite network during transmission by exploiting the hardware, software, and protocol vulnerabilities. Compared to single-domain defenses, cooperative defense at the IoT devices, IoT access network, and satellite transmission network provides fine-granularity defense against cross-domain intelligent attacks. However, quantifying cross-domain impacts and tilting incentive misalignment among different participants remain significant challenges, making systematic cooperative defense development a complex task. To address this, we develop a tripartite security game framework to characterize the impacts of attacks and defense methods across both the terrestrial and satellite domains. Leveraging this game model, we devise flow pricing to optimally motivate the IoT network operator (IoT-NO) to prevent malicious packet infiltration into the satellite domain. Subsequently, we propose efficient learning algorithms enabling both the IoT-NO to ascertain their ideal flow sampling strategies and the satellite service provider (SAT-SP) to determine optimal flow pricing. The simulation results corroborate the effectiveness of the consolidated game in counteracting cross-domain cyber attacks and facilitating cooperative defense between the IoT-NO and the SAT-SP with nonaligned incentives.
tldr: This paper proposes a tripartite security game framework for cooperative defense against cross-domain cyber attacks in satellite-enabled IoT, focusing on incentive alignment and flow pricing.
motivation: Satellite-enabled IoT is vulnerable to cross-domain cyber attacks, and cooperative defense is challenging due to incentive misalignment among participants.
method: The authors develop a tripartite security game model and design flow pricing mechanisms, along with learning algorithms for optimal strategies.
result: Simulations show the game framework effectively counteracts cross-domain attacks and facilitates cooperative defense between IoT network operators and satellite service providers.
conclusion: The proposed game-based approach provides a systematic way to coordinate defense across terrestrial and satellite domains despite nonaligned incentives.

title: New Lower And Upper Bounds For The Grothendieck Constant

abstract: ArXiv:2608.11158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish new bounds on the Grothendieck constant [MATH]: \[ {11} \le K_G \le {2\log(1+\sqrt2)} - 10^{-4}. \] Methodologically, our lower bound approach differs from previous works by establishing limitations on the asymptotically optimal Krivine schemes, rather than giving explicit constructions of gap instances. Our upper bound is obtained by proposing and analyzing the first asymptotic construction of rounding schemes, whereas previous works only consider low-dimensional schemes. Together, these bounds determine the previously unknown tenths digit of [MATH] to be [MATH]. The bounds were discovered by a long-running collaborative effort of humans and a long-horizon AI research system that we engineered.
tldr: This paper establishes new lower and upper bounds for the Grothendieck constant, a fundamental constant in functional analysis and optimization, using novel proof techniques and AI-assisted discovery.

title: How To Verify Consistency Of Probabilistic Claims
authors: Orr Paradise, Oliver Richardson, Yoshua Bengio, Shafi Goldwasser
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a probabilistic predictor answers many conditional-probability queries, are its answers self-consistent, and can this be verified in polynomial time? This problem is of interest for AI safety, where safety is derived from honesty about probabilistic predictions of unwanted outcomes potentially caused by an AI action. We construct an interactive PCP as follows. Let a predictive model be specified by a probability circuit P and a circuit Q which outputs confidence in predictions. Together, P and Q implicitly specify exponentially many probabilistic claims. We show a protocol in which a polynomial-time verifier can verify the approximate consistency of (P,Q). The verifier is given the pair of circuits (P,Q), which it evaluates at only a few points; alongside them it is given a proof oracle, an encoding of a witnessing probability distribution allegedly consistent with the predictions of (P,Q), which it reads at a few locations while interacting with a single untrusted prover. En route, we must ensure the existence of a sparse witnessing distribution consistent with the model's predictions. To do so, we first consider witness distributions for the consistency of explicit probabilistic claims, rather than claims specified by a predictor: say m claims, each of the form Pr[Y = 1 | X = x] = p, over n Boolean variables. Building on work initiated by Nilsson (Artif. Intell., 1986), we place l_2-approximate probabilistic consistency of explicit claims in NP, with certificates of length O(mn + log B) in the input bit-precision B; we further show how a small additive completeness-soundness gap removes the dependence on B. Together these results provide a complexity-theoretic foundation for certifying the self-consistency of probabilistic predictors. We view our interactive PCP as a first step toward training predictive models to prove their own consistency.
tldr: This paper introduces an interactive PCP protocol to verify the consistency of probabilistic claims made by a predictor, with complexity-theoretic results for explicit claims.
motivation: The authors aim to address AI safety by ensuring that probabilistic predictors are self-consistent, which is crucial for trustworthy predictions about unwanted outcomes.
method: They construct an interactive PCP where a verifier checks consistency by querying a proof oracle encoding a witnessing distribution, and they prove NP membership for l2-approximate consistency of explicit claims.
result: They show that consistency of explicit claims can be certified in NP with certificates of length O(mn + log B), and that a small completeness-soundness gap removes dependence on B.
conclusion: The work provides a complexity-theoretic foundation for certifying self-consistency of probabilistic predictors, serving as a step toward training models to prove their own consistency.

title: Certified Misty-State Rewriting (a Question-and-Answer Guide)
authors: Dan-Adrian German Tony Newton
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10024v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum mechanics is difficult to teach because its conceptual content and mathematical notation usually arrive together. Rudolph's misty-state language was designed to decouple those burdens; basis states are visual objects, clouds represent superposition, gates act by elementary replacement rules, and destructive interference appears as cancellation rather than as matrix calculation. An elementary ``misty-state'' language can make quantum circuits accessible to students before they master complex linear algebra. Development presented here was initiated/led by the first author. The contribution is not a replacement for complete graphical calculi such as ZX or sum-over-paths. It is a source-specific bridge from an intuitive educational notation to a mathematically explicit, executable, and falsifiable semantics.
tldr: This paper presents an educational tool using misty-state notation to teach quantum circuits without requiring linear algebra.
motivation: Quantum mechanics is hard to teach because conceptual content and mathematical notation are introduced together; the misty-state language aims to decouple them.
method: The authors develop an elementary misty-state language with visual basis states, clouds for superposition, and replacement rules for gates, and provide a bridge to explicit executable semantics.
result: The contribution is a source-specific educational bridge, not a replacement for complete graphical calculi like ZX or sum-over-paths.
conclusion: The paper offers a pedagogical approach to make quantum circuits accessible to students before they master complex linear algebra.

title: Logit-Boundary Geometric Belief Interfaces And Sparse Sheaf-Enclave Protocols: A Self-Contained Substrate For Secure Network Electronic Health Record (ehr) Interoperability
authors: Thomas Huang Alvin Spivey
abstract: ArXiv:2608.10300v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electronic health-record interoperability is a boundary problem: legacy systems, generative models, terminology services, identity systems, and human reviewers may each expose rich internal states, while operational exchange requires a narrow shared interface of typed claims, bounded uncertainty, provenance, and explicit admission or abstention. This paper details a mathematical and engineering architecture for that interface. The organizing idea is the logit boundary: a discovery model may propose pre-threshold scores over a local categorical decision, but a deterministic judgment substrate decides whether the proposal is admissible, requires review, or must be quarantined before any Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) transaction is constructed. The resulting Geometric Belief Interface (GBI) combines finite boundary semantics, local Dirichlet evidence, cellular-sheaf and mapping-cone diagnostics, advisory geometric audit charts, and a Decentralized Cryptographic Sheaf-Enclave (DCSE) protocol sketch for fail-closed deployment. The framework does not establish clinical truth, global representation alignment, or end-to-end safety; it defines certificate-producing checks at a model-to-system boundary. A companion frozen synthetic benchmark, GBI BoundaryBench v0.1, evaluated Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on 256 held-out tasks across three evidence modes (768 canonical executions). All executions completed, but none produced an output accepted by the benchmark contract: 369 were rejected during safe parsing and 399 during schema validation, yielding zero coverage and deterministic quarantine. This empirical result is deliberately narrow - one 4B open-weight model under one frozen interface - and is reported as evidence about the admission boundary, not as a general claim about LLM capability or clinical safety. A Julia appendix verifies numerical certificates using standard libraries.
tldr: This paper proposes a mathematical and engineering architecture for secure EHR interoperability using logit boundaries and sheaf-theoretic protocols, but it is not aligned with the user's research interests.
motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of secure and reliable electronic health record (EHR) interoperability, focusing on boundary interfaces between AI models and healthcare systems.
method: It introduces a Geometric Belief Interface (GBI) combining finite boundary semantics, Dirichlet evidence, cellular-sheaf diagnostics, and a Decentralized Cryptographic Sheaf-Enclave (DCSE) protocol, with a synthetic benchmark evaluation.
result: The benchmark showed zero accepted outputs from a 4B model, leading to deterministic quarantine, but this is presented as narrow evidence about the admission boundary.
conclusion: The framework provides certificate-producing checks at the model-to-system boundary but does not claim clinical truth or general safety.

Author(s): Jean Barbier, Francesco Camilli, Minh-Toan Nguyen, Mauro Pastore, and Rudy Skerk

Using statistical physics and random matrix theory, researchers derive the generalization error of a deep fully connected neural network and uncover the mechanisms governing its behavior as feature learning progressively propagates across layers.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031014] Published Wed Jul 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses statistical physics and random matrix theory to analyze the generalization error of deep neural networks near the interpolation threshold.
motivation: Understanding the generalization behavior of deep neural networks is a central question in machine learning, and statistical physics provides tools to analyze high-dimensional models.
method: The authors derive the generalization error of a deep fully connected neural network using techniques from statistical physics and random matrix theory, focusing on the regime near interpolation.
result: They uncover mechanisms governing the behavior of the network as feature learning propagates across layers, providing insights into the interpolation peak and double descent.
conclusion: The work contributes to the theoretical understanding of deep learning, but it is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Identifying Geometric Third-Order Nonlinear Transport In Disordered Materials
authors: Zhen-Hao Gong, Zhi-Hao Wei, Hai-Zhou Lu, And X. C. Xie
abstract:

A theoretical data-analysis tool resolves the chaotic interpretation of nonlinear electronic transport data, providing a structured method to extract quantum geometric properties from realistic materials.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031012] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a theoretical data-analysis tool to extract quantum geometric properties from nonlinear transport data in disordered materials.
motivation: The interpretation of nonlinear electronic transport data in disordered materials is chaotic, and there is a need for a structured method to extract quantum geometric properties.
method: The authors develop a theoretical data-analysis tool that resolves the chaotic interpretation by providing a structured method to extract quantum geometric properties from realistic materials.
result: The tool enables the identification of geometric third-order nonlinear transport in disordered materials.
conclusion: The proposed method offers a way to extract quantum geometric information from transport measurements, potentially useful for characterizing materials.

motivation: The study aims to detect a fractional topological insulator state, a novel quantum phase of matter.
method: Pump-probe modulation spectroscopy was used to measure the optical response of a MoTe2 bilayer superlattice.
result: An out-of-plane antiferromagnetic response was observed, providing evidence for the fractional topological insulator state.
conclusion: The findings support the existence of fractional topological insulators in twisted MoTe2, but the work is primarily a condensed matter experiment without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Covariant Path Integrals For Quantum Fields Backreacting On Classical Space-Time
authors: Jonathan Oppenheim And Zachary Weller-Davies
abstract:
Author(s): Jonathan Oppenheim and Zachary Weller-Davies

Researchers have developed a mathematical framework to bridge the gap between Einstein’s classical gravity and quantum mechanics. Their theory allows matter to remain quantum while space-time stays classical, offering a way to test if space and time truly require a quantum explanation.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031007] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a covariant path integral framework for quantum fields backreacting on classical spacetime, aiming to unify quantum mechanics and gravity without quantizing spacetime.
motivation: The authors aim to address the long-standing problem of reconciling quantum mechanics with general relativity by allowing matter to be quantum while spacetime remains classical, potentially offering a testable alternative to full quantum gravity.
method: They develop a covariant path integral formalism that describes the dynamics of quantum fields interacting with a classical spacetime background, incorporating backreaction effects.
result: The framework provides a consistent mathematical description of the backreaction, potentially leading to observable predictions that could distinguish between classical and quantum spacetime.
conclusion: The work offers a novel approach to quantum gravity that may be experimentally testable, but it is far removed from the specific research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

method: They develop SciExplorer, a large-language-model-based agent that iteratively proposes experiments, analyzes data, and refines models of physical systems.
result: The agent successfully uncovers underlying models for diverse physical systems without fine-tuning, demonstrating its generality and effectiveness.
conclusion: The work showcases the potential of AI agents in physics research, but its focus on automation and discovery is outside the core interests of quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

A nonperturbative quantization framework for chiral solitons in spin chains demonstrates that they condense into a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid, appearing as low-energy excitations above the ferromagnetic phase and becoming detectable via inelastic neutron scattering.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021056] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a nonperturbative quantization framework for chiral solitons in spin chains, showing they condense into a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid and are detectable via neutron scattering.
motivation: To understand the quantum dynamics of chiral solitons in spin chains, which are topological excitations with potential relevance to quantum magnetism.
method: The authors develop a nonperturbative quantization approach for chiral solitons and analyze their condensation into a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid.
result: Chiral solitons appear as low-energy excitations above the ferromagnetic phase and can be observed via inelastic neutron scattering.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for chiral solitons, but it is primarily a condensed matter physics study without direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

tldr: This paper uses fuzzy sphere regularization to study free and interacting fermionic conformal field theories in three dimensions, uncovering emergent supersymmetry.
motivation: To understand non-perturbative aspects of fermionic CFTs and explore emergent symmetries using a noncommutative geometry approach.
method: The authors employ the fuzzy sphere, a noncommutative discretization of the sphere, to simulate fermionic CFTs and analyze their spectra and correlation functions.
result: They find evidence for emergent supersymmetry in certain interacting fermionic CFTs, and demonstrate the effectiveness of the fuzzy sphere method for studying such theories.
conclusion: The fuzzy sphere provides a powerful numerical tool for investigating fermionic CFTs, and the observed emergent supersymmetry may have implications for strongly coupled quantum field theories.

title: Are Neural Networks Collision Resistant?
authors: Marco Benedetti, Andrej Bogdanov, Enrico M. Malatesta, Marc Mézard, Gianmarco Perrupato, Alon Rosen, Nikolaj I. Schwartzbach, And Riccardo Zecchina
